questions.prompt: Find the conjugate needed to simplify \\(\frac{1}{3-2i}\\).
questions.answer:
The denominator is \\(3-2i\\).
Its conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part, so the needed conjugate is \\(3+2i\\).

Multiply by the conjugate \\(1-i\\):
\\(\frac{1}{1+i}\\cdot\frac{1-i}{1-i}=\frac{1-i}{1-i^2}\\).
The denominator is \\(2\\).
So the result is \\(\frac12-\frac12 i\\).

Multiply numerator and denominator by \\(1+i\\).
Numerator: \\((3+i)(1+i)=3+3i+i+i^2=2+4i\\).
Denominator: \\((1-i)(1+i)=2\\).
So the quotient is \\(1+2i\\).

Multiply by \\(3-i\\).
Numerator: \\((2-5i)(3-i)=6-2i-15i+5i^2=1-17i\\).
Denominator: \\((3+i)(3-i)=10\\).
So the answer is \\(\frac{1}{10}-\frac{17}{10}i\\).

Multiply by \\(2-2i\\).
Numerator: \\((-1+4i)(2-2i)=-2+2i+8i-8i^2=6+10i\\).
Denominator: \\(2^2+2^2=8\\).
So the quotient is \\(\frac34+\frac54i\\).

For \\(a+bi=5+2i\\), \\(c+di=1+3i\\).
Real numerator: \\(ac+bd=5+6=11\\).
Imaginary numerator: \\(bc-ad=2-15=-13\\).
Denominator: \\(c^2+d^2=1+9=10\\).
So \\(\frac{5+2i}{1+3i}=\frac{11}{10}-\frac{13}{10}i\\).

First square the numerator: \\((1+i)^2=1+2i+i^2=2i\\).
Then \\(\frac{2i}{1-i}\\cdot\frac{1+i}{1+i}=\frac{2i+2i^2}{2}\\).
This is \\(\frac{-2+2i}{2}=-1+i\\).

Multiply the proposed reciprocal by \\(2-i\\).
\\((2-i)(\frac25+\frac15i)=\frac45+\frac25i-\frac25i-\frac15i^2\\).
The imaginary terms cancel and \\(-\frac15i^2=\frac15\\).
The product is \\(1\\), so the reciprocal is correct.

questions.prompt: Explain why the denominator becomes real when dividing by \\(c+di\\) using its conjugate.
questions.answer:
Multiply the denominator by \\(c-di\\).
\\((c+di)(c-di)=c^2-cdi+cdi-d^2i^2\\).
The imaginary terms cancel.
Since \\(i^2=-1\\), the result is \\(c^2+d^2\\), a real number.

Multiply both sides by \\(1+i\\).
\\(a+bi=(2-i)(1+i)\\).
Expand: \\(2+2i-i-i^2=3+i\\).
Thus \\(a=3\\) and \\(b=1\\).

Multiply by \\(1+i\\): \\(\frac{(1+ti)(1+i)}{2}\\).
Numerator: \\(1+i+ti+ti^2=(1-t)+(1+t)i\\).
The quotient is real when \\(1+t=0\\).
So \\(t=-1\\).

questions.prompt: For which real \\(t\\) is \\(\frac{t+i}{2+i}\\) purely imaginary?
questions.answer:
Multiply by \\(2-i\\).
Numerator: \\((t+i)(2-i)=2t-ti+2i-i^2=(2t+1)+(2-t)i\\).
Denominator is \\(5\\).
Purely imaginary means real part zero: \\(2t+1=0\\).
Thus \\(t=-\frac12\\).

questions.prompt: Find all real \\(t\\) for which \\(\frac{2+ti}{t-i}\\) is real, with \\(t\neq0\\) not assumed.
questions.answer:
The denominator \\(t-i\\) is never zero for real \\(t\\).
Multiply by \\(t+i\\): numerator \\((2+ti)(t+i)=2t+2i+t^2i+ti^2\\).
This is \\(t+(2+t^2)i\\).
Denominator is \\(t^2+1\\).
For a real quotient, \\(2+t^2=0\\), which has no real solution.
So no real \\(t\\) works.

questions.prompt: A learner simplifies \\(\frac{1}{3+4i}\\) as \\(\frac13+\frac14i\\). Diagnose the error and find the reciprocal.
questions.answer:
You cannot divide the real and imaginary parts separately.
Use the conjugate: \\(\frac{1}{3+4i}\\cdot\frac{3-4i}{3-4i}=\frac{3-4i}{9+16}\\).
So the reciprocal is \\(\frac3{25}-\frac4{25}i\\).

Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \\(a-bi\\).
\\(\frac{1}{a+bi}=\frac{a-bi}{(a+bi)(a-bi)}\\).
The denominator is \\(a^2+b^2\\).
Since \\(a+bi\neq0\\), \\(a^2+b^2\neq0\\).
Therefore \\(\frac{1}{a+bi}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}\\).

questions.prompt: Explain why division by \\(0+0i\\) is not allowed, using the conjugate method.
questions.answer:
The conjugate method would put \\(a^2+b^2\\) in the denominator for \\(a+bi\\).
For \\(0+0i\\), this denominator is \\(0^2+0^2=0\\).
Division by zero is undefined, so division by the zero complex number is not allowed.
